project.name: tula-auth
project.description: Tula Auth is an open-source, self-hostable authentication and user management platform: a Bun + TypeScript monorepo whose Hono/PostgreSQL (Drizzle ORM) auth API publishes an OpenAPI contract from which the web, Expo, Swift and Kotlin SDKs, the operator dashboard, the CLI and the MCP server are generated or tested. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

nodes.name: errors.ts

nodes.name: parseConfig

nodes.name: defineConfig
nodes.summary: Identity helper that types and returns the config exported from tula.config.ts.

nodes.name: selectEnvironment
nodes.summary: Picks the named environment from a config, or the only one, throwing environment_required or environment_unknown otherwise.

nodes.name: resolveSecret
nodes.summary: Resolves a SecretRef to its value from the supplied variables, throwing config.secret_missing that names only the variable.

nodes.name: requiredSecrets
nodes.summary: Lists the secret references a set of providers needs so callers can check them before applying.

nodes.name: providerSecret

nodes.name: canonical
nodes.summary: Recursively orders object keys so a config serialises identically in any key order.

nodes.name: withoutUnusedDefaults
nodes.summary: Strips optional sections left at their defaults so an environment that does not mention newer features hashes as it did before.

nodes.name: hashEnvironmentConfig
nodes.summary: Computes a sha256 fingerprint of one environment's config with secrets as variable names only, used by apply and diff to record which file version is in force.

nodes.name: ConfigError
nodes.summary: The one error the package throws, carrying a code and path-named issues and a safe toJSON that never exposes file or environment values.

nodes.name: isConfigError
nodes.summary: Type guard recognising a ConfigError, including across module copies.

nodes.name: invalidConfig
nodes.summary: Builds a config.invalid ConfigError from a list of issues.

nodes.name: loadConfig
nodes.summary: Imports a config file by path (running it), maps a missing file or failed import to ConfigError, and returns the validated default export with its resolved path.

nodes.name: parse
nodes.summary: Parses argv into positional arguments and long/short flags, rejecting unknown options with a UsageError.

nodes.summary: Reads a port flag, accepting only a 1-to-5-digit number.

nodes.name: chooseFramework
nodes.summary: Returns the framework given on the command line or asks on a terminal for one of the supported frameworks.

nodes.name: main
nodes.summary: Runs create-tula: reads name and options, scaffolds the project, and reports next steps; never throws, never exits and never prints a secret.

nodes.name: processIo
nodes.summary: Builds the real-run surroundings from the process streams, cwd and a readline prompt on a terminal.

nodes.name: needsTulaRepo

nodes.summary: Scaffolds a Tula project: Compose file, .env with generated secrets, config, README and the chosen example app, writing nothing unless everything can be.

nodes.name: ScaffoldError
nodes.summary: Error thrown for an unusable name or option, a non-empty directory, a missing tarball or a symbolic link in the way.

nodes.name: docs.ts

nodes.name: snippets.ts

nodes.summary: Reads a package manifest and resolves its public entry points (specifier and source file) for the reference page.

nodes.summary: Creates the ts-morph compiler program over the entry-point files used to read exported symbols and JSDoc.

nodes.name: shown
nodes.summary: Returns a repository-relative path for display and map keys.

nodes.name: withoutBody
nodes.summary: Cuts a declaration down to its signature by dropping the body.

nodes.name: isHidden
nodes.summary: Decides whether an export is excluded from the reference (for example internal or hidden by tag).

nodes.name: classSignature
nodes.summary: Renders the signature of a class declaration for the reference.

nodes.name: constantSignature
nodes.summary: Renders the signature of an exported constant, including its type.

nodes.name: describe
nodes.summary: Builds a printable description (kind, signature, summary) of an exported symbol from its declarations.

nodes.name: tagText
nodes.summary: Extracts the text of a JSDoc tag.

nodes.name: renderTags
nodes.summary: Renders `@param`, `@returns`, `@throws` and `@example` tags as Markdown.

nodes.name: renderEntry
nodes.summary: Renders one exported symbol as a Markdown section with signature, summary and tags, and records it as undocumented when it has no summary.

nodes.summary: Builds every docs/reference page (packages plus the native SDK pages) as a map from path to text, and the list of undocumented exports.

nodes.name: markdownFiles
nodes.summary: Lists the Markdown files under docs/ and the READMEs whose snippet blocks are filled.

nodes.name: current
nodes.summary: Reads the file currently on disk (or empty) to compare with the wanted text.

nodes.name: codeOnly
nodes.summary: Replaces comments and string contents of Swift or Kotlin source with blanks of equal length, so later scans match only code.

nodes.name: matchDeclaration
nodes.summary: Matches a source line against the declaration patterns of a language and returns its kind and name.

nodes.name: readSignature
nodes.summary: Reads a declaration signature from its first line to the opening brace or end, across wrapped lines.

nodes.name: tidy
nodes.summary: Normalises whitespace of a captured signature.

nodes.name: namesOf
nodes.summary: Joins the names of the enclosing containers into a qualified name.

nodes.name: documentationOf
nodes.summary: Collects the doc comment lines that precede a declaration and counts one with none as undocumented.

nodes.name: commentDepthChange
nodes.summary: Computes the change in block-comment nesting for a line (Swift and Kotlin comments nest).

nodes.name: dedent
nodes.summary: Removes the common leading indentation from a block of text.

nodes.name: isInside
nodes.summary: Tells whether a file lies inside a directory after path resolution.

nodes.summary: Rejects paths that must never be copied into docs (secrets, env files, git data).

layers.name: API Runtime & Composition
layers.description: The shell of the Hono auth server in apps/api: createApp and its lazy route registration, the Bun.serve and webhook-worker entrypoints, the env schema, the composition root (container.ts) that picks an adapter for every port, the job scheduler, the error envelope and the package's own build files and scripts. It wires the HTTP surface, domain modules and adapters together and is the only place that knows all three.

layers.name: API HTTP Surface
layers.description: What a request passes through before any business logic: each module's thin router (describeRoute, validator, auth) and its Zod request/response schemas, plus the middleware for publishable, secret and agent keys, sessions, CORS and rate limits. Routers delegate to the domain services and take their shared shapes from the contract.

layers.name: API Domain Modules
layers.description: The business logic of each feature under apps/api/src/modules as exported service functions that take Deps: the flow engine and its transitions, sessions, passwords, MFA, passkeys, OAuth, webhooks, hooks, retention, notices, email and SMS wording. Called by the routers and the background jobs; reaches storage and the outside world only through ports.

layers.name: API Ports
layers.description: The interfaces the domain depends on (apps/api/src/ports): stores and repositories, the mailer, clock, rate limiter, lockout, key store and locks. Domain modules import these; adapters implement them.

layers.name: API Adapters
layers.description: Implementations of the ports by technology (apps/api/src/adapters): memory for unit tests, Postgres through Drizzle, Redis for state shared between instances, and the OAuth, SMS, mail, breach-check, cache and system adapters. Chosen only by the composition root, and built on the database package.

layers.name: API Shared Library
layers.description: Cross-cutting helpers in apps/api/src/lib that modules, middleware and adapters all import: crypto, keyed hashes, the secret box, TOTP, WebAuthn, DPoP, the guarded outbound request, the logger, actors and client-IP handling. It depends on nothing above it.

layers.name: Shared Contract
layers.description: packages/contract: the Zod schemas, flow protocol, error codes, token claims, session profiles, theme and message templates that the API and every TypeScript SDK import, and from which the OpenAPI snapshot and generated types follow. The base of the dependency graph.

layers.name: Database Schema & Tenancy
layers.description: packages/db: the Drizzle table definitions with their tenant columns and row-level-security mixins, the client, the withTenant and advisory-lock helpers, and the migrate, seed and drift-check scripts. Used by the API's Postgres adapters.

layers.name: Core Client SDK
layers.description: packages/core: the headless TypeScript client (flows, session, single-flight refresh) that the React, Next.js and Expo SDKs are built on, with the generators that turn openapi.json into its types and into the Swift and Kotlin generated sources.

layers.name: React & Next.js SDKs
layers.description: packages/react (provider, hooks and prebuilt sign-in, sign-up, reset and account components with one themeable stylesheet) and packages/nextjs (route handler, request interceptor and server helpers for the App Router). Both sit on the core client and the contract.

layers.name: Expo SDKs
layers.description: packages/expo, the headless React Native SDK with secure-store sessions, passkey, provider and device-key adapters and a config plugin; and packages/expo-screens, an Expo native module that wraps the SwiftUI and Compose screens of the native SDKs.

layers.name: Native SDKs (Swift & Kotlin)
layers.description: native/swift (the TulaAuth client and the TulaAuthUI SwiftUI screens) and native/android (tula-auth, its Android adapters, and the Compose screens' model and drawing modules), with their Gradle and SwiftPM build files and the fixtures that run their journeys against the real API. Their types are generated from the contract by the core SDK's scripts.

layers.name: Operator Tooling
layers.description: What an operator or an agent drives a deployment with: packages/admin (the typed /v1/admin client), packages/config (tula.config.ts), packages/cli (the tula executable), packages/mcp (the MCP server) and packages/create-tula (the project scaffolder). All of them talk to the API's admin and instance routes.

layers.name: Dashboard App Shell
layers.description: The frame of the operator dashboard in apps/dashboard: the Vite entry, TanStack Router route files, shared components, the generated API hooks and fetch layer, client state, utilities, and the generate scripts and build config. Routes mount the feature screens.

layers.name: Dashboard Features
layers.description: The screens of the dashboard by area (apps/dashboard/src/features): users, settings, API keys, webhooks, hooks, message wording, SMS, native apps, proposals, workspaces, diagnostics, the audit log, the dashboard's own sign-in session and its navigation shell. Each uses the shell's components and API hooks to call the API's admin and instance routes.

layers.name: Example Apps
layers.description: Runnable or compiled sample apps under examples/: React + Vite, Next.js App Router, Expo, SwiftUI, Compose, the core playground, the docs snippets and an example tula.config.ts. They consume the SDKs as a developer would, and are what the browser tests and create-tula's templates are made from.

layers.name: Conformance & End-to-End Testing
layers.description: packages/conformance and conformance/ (the language-neutral scenario runner, its format and the client-journey list every SDK is held to) and e2e/ (Playwright with the real API in process, and the fixture server for the Kotlin journeys). It exercises the API and the SDKs from outside.

layers.name: Infrastructure & CI
layers.description: How the system is packaged and run: the API Dockerfile and its stages, docker-compose services, the nginx proxy and Postgres role bootstrap under docker/, the GitHub workflows and Dependabot config, the git hooks, and the self-host and worker-check scripts.

layers.name: Workspace Config & Release Tooling
layers.description: The monorepo's own machinery: root package.json, Turborepo, Biome and bunfig settings, .env.example, the shared tsconfig bases, and scripts/ that build, pack and check the publishable packages and generate the SDK reference.

layers.name: Documentation
layers.description: The guides under docs/ (quickstart, self-hosting, per-method and per-provider pages, SDK guides), the root README, glossary and contributor standards, and the pull-request template. Package READMEs stay with the package they describe.

tour.title: Project Overview and Layout
tour.description: Start with the README: Tula Auth is a self-hostable authentication and user-management server with web, Expo and native SDKs, a dashboard, a CLI and an MCP server, all in one Bun + TypeScript monorepo. The root package.json and turbo.json show how the workspace is split into apps/, packages/, native/ and examples/ and how root scripts fan out through Turborepo. The glossary and the docs index give you the vocabulary (environment, flow, attempt, publishable and secret key) that every later step uses.

tour.title: The Contract: One Source of Truth
tour.description: packages/contract holds the Zod schemas, the flow protocol, the error codes, the token claims and the session profiles that the API and every TypeScript SDK import. Read flow.ts first: it defines the flow steps (needs_password, needs_first_factor, complete and so on) the server returns instead of telling a client which screen to draw. error-codes.ts and environment-settings.ts define the stable error vocabulary and the per-environment settings; the OpenAPI document generated from the running API is what the SDK types, the dashboard hooks and the native types are later derived from.
tour.languageLesson: Zod schemas are runtime validators and static types at once: `z.infer<typeof Schema>` gives the TypeScript type, so one declaration serves request validation, the OpenAPI document and every importer's types.

tour.title: Booting the API
tour.description: With the contract in mind, follow the server's start. server.ts is the Bun.serve entrypoint: it parses the environment with the Zod schema in env.ts (failing fast on a bad value), asks container.ts for the dependencies, and hands them to createApp in index.ts. createApp builds the Hono app without listening, installs the middleware and registers each module's router with a lazy import, which is why tests and embedded use can mount the same app. dependencies.ts defines Deps, the bag of ports every service takes, and is the most imported file in the repository.

tour.title: Keys, Middleware and Route Groups
tour.description: Before any business logic a request passes the middleware that decides who is calling. /v1/client/* takes a publishable key that resolves the project and environment; /v1/admin/* takes a secret key or the dashboard's session; /v1/agent/* takes an agent key; /v1/instance/* takes the instance admin token. session-auth verifies an access token without a database hit, rate-limit guards every credential-accepting route, and cors decides whether an origin may use cookies. Knowing which group a route sits in tells you what it may trust.

tour.title: Errors and the OpenAPI Surface
tour.description: Every failure leaves the API in one shape. Services throw the ServiceException subclasses or AuthError from exceptions.ts, and handlers.ts turns them (and validation failures) into the contract's error envelope with a stable dot-namespaced code. openapi.ts holds the shared responses and security requirements that each route's describeRoute spreads in, which is what keeps the generated document complete. This is the plumbing the module pattern in the next step relies on.

tour.title: The Module Pattern: The Flow Engine
tour.description: Every feature lives in modules/<name>/ as a thin router.ts, a service.ts of exported functions whose first argument is deps, and a schema.ts of Zod shapes. The flow module is the worked example and the heart of the product: router.ts validates and delegates, service.ts runs sign-up, sign-in and reset attempts, and transitions.ts is one pure function, nextStatus, that decides the next step for every kind, status and event. factor/service.ts is the registry of first and second factors, so adding a sign-in method means adding an entry there rather than editing the transition function or any SDK.
tour.languageLesson: Keeping the state machine a pure function (inputs in, next status out, no I/O) lets a table test enumerate every combination; the service around it does the I/O and stays easy to reason about.

tour.title: Sessions, Tokens and Signing Keys
tour.description: A flow that reaches `complete` ends in a session. session/service.ts issues short-lived EdDSA access tokens and opaque, single-use, rotating refresh tokens, and revokes a whole token family when one is reused; cookies.ts is the only place the refresh cookie is set. jwks/service.ts owns each environment's signing keys and publishes the public halves so that a backend can verify a token offline. lib/crypto.ts and lib/secret-box.ts supply the random tokens, hashing, constant-time comparison and the sealing of private keys.

tour.title: Ports, Adapters and the Composition Root
tour.description: Services never touch a database handle: they call ports, interfaces in src/ports such as the session store, the rate limiter and the clock. Each port has a memory adapter for unit tests, a Postgres adapter for production, and for state shared between instances (rate limits, lockout, revoked sessions) a Redis adapter. container.ts is the only file that chooses among them, from the environment; testing.ts builds the same Deps from memory adapters and a fixed clock. Compare the three session-related adapters here to see one port implemented three ways.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript interfaces are structural: an adapter implements a port simply by having the right shape, and `Pick<Deps, 'sessions' | 'clock'>` lets a service declare exactly the ports it needs.

tour.title: Database Schema and Tenancy
tour.description: The Postgres adapters are built on packages/db. Tables are Drizzle definitions under src/schema, assembled from mixins (a uuid v7 primary key, timestamps) and tenant-columns.ts, which gives every tenant table project_id and environment_id plus a fail-closed row-level-security policy. tenant.ts exports withTenant, the wrapper every tenant query runs inside, and docker/postgres/init.sql creates the roles so that the API connects as a role that cannot bypass RLS. Read users.ts and sessions.ts as examples of the tables behind the stores from the previous step.
tour.languageLesson: Row-level security moves the tenant filter into the database: a policy compares each row's environment to a per-transaction setting, so a query that forgets its WHERE clause returns nothing instead of another tenant's rows.

tour.title: Background Jobs, Webhooks and the Worker
tour.description: Not everything happens on a request. jobs.ts is the one place background jobs are put on a timer, and process.ts decides which jobs an API process or a worker process runs. retention/service.ts deletes rows that have expired, in batches through store methods; webhook/service.ts takes events from the outbox and delivers them, signed and retried, through lib/outbound.ts, the guarded request that refuses private addresses and redirects. worker.ts is the entrypoint that runs delivery as a service of its own, and the job-lock port lets only one process through each round.

tour.title: The Core Client SDK
tour.description: Now cross to the client side. packages/core is the headless TypeScript client every other JS SDK is built on: client.ts assembles it, transport.ts sends requests with the publishable key, flows.ts drives the server's flow steps from step 6, and session.ts keeps the tokens and refreshes them single-flight so that concurrent calls share one rotation. Its API types are not hand-written: scripts/openapi-types.ts generates them from the contract's OpenAPI document, which is how the client cannot drift from the server.

tour.title: React and Next.js SDKs
tour.description: packages/react wraps the core client in a provider (context.tsx), hooks such as use-sign-in and use-flow, and prebuilt components: flow-screens.tsx renders whichever step the server returned, so the UI follows the flow protocol rather than encoding its own. packages/nextjs adds the server half for the App Router: a same-origin route handler, a request interceptor that verifies sessions offline against the JWKS, and server helpers. The Vite example app shows the components composed into a real page.
tour.languageLesson: React context plus custom hooks is the pattern here: one provider holds the client, and hooks like useSignIn read it, so components stay free of wiring.

tour.title: Expo and the Native Swift and Kotlin SDKs
tour.description: Mobile follows the same protocol with platform storage. packages/expo is the core client with its refresh token in the device's secure store, plus a provider and hooks. The native SDKs are separate clients: TulaClient.swift and TulaClient.kt implement flows and sessions by hand, while their API types, error codes and theme are generated from the same OpenAPI document by packages/core/scripts/native. TulaAuthModel in each SDK is what the SwiftUI and Compose screens decide, kept apart from what draws them.

tour.title: Operator Tooling and the Dashboard
tour.description: Operators reach the /v1/admin and /v1/instance groups from step 4 through several tools. packages/admin is the typed, generated client that holds a secret key; packages/config defines tula.config.ts, an environment's settings as code; the CLI's diff and apply commands compare that file with the server and change it; packages/mcp serves read-only and propose tools to AI assistants; create-tula scaffolds a project. apps/dashboard is the same admin API as a Vite + React single-page app: main.tsx and the app shell set it up, and its hooks are generated from the OpenAPI document by Orval.

tour.title: Conformance, E2E, CI and Releasing
tour.description: Finally, how the whole is held together. packages/conformance runs language-neutral JSON scenarios over HTTP, in process and against a live server, and client-journeys.json lists what each client's test suite does about every scenario, so server and SDKs are tested against one behaviour. e2e/server.ts starts the real API on memory adapters for the Playwright browser tests. The Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml package the API with Postgres and Redis for self-hosting, ci.yml runs the full verify gate, and docs/releasing.md explains how the publishable packages are built and checked (nothing is published yet).
tour.languageLesson: A multi-stage Dockerfile installs and builds in early stages and copies only what the server needs into the release stage; in GitHub Actions, separate jobs run in parallel and each lists its steps in order.
